en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Familiarity from the Section of Puzzling Questions (Meṇḍakapañha)
11. The Question of Teacher and Non-Teacher “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One: ‘I have no teacher;’”
‘There is no one equal to me;
in this world with its devas,
there is no individual who is my peer.’”
And again it was said:
“Thus indeed, monks, Āḷāra Kālāma, though he was my teacher, placed me—the pupil—on an equal footing with himself and honored me with great honor.
If, venerable Nāgasena, this was spoken by the Tathāgata—
‘I have no teacher; one equal to me is not found.

In this world with its devas, there is no rival to me’—if that is so, monks, then the statement that ‘Āḷāra Kālāma, though being my teacher, placed me, his pupil, on an equality with himself’ is false.
If it was said by the Tathāgata:

“Thus indeed, bhikkhus, Āḷāra Kālāma, though he was my teacher, placed me—who was his pupil—on an equal footing with himself,” then that statement of yours, “I have no teacher; there is none equal to me;
in this world with its devas, there is no one who is my counterpart,” must also be false.
“This too is a double-edged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.
“Indeed, Great King, this was also spoken by the Tathāgata:
‘I have no teacher...’”
‘No one equal to me is found;
in this world with its devas,
there is no person who is my peer.’
And it was said:
“Thus, monks, Āḷāra Kālāma, though he was my teacher, placed me—a mere pupil—on an equal footing with himself and honored me with sublime honor.
Now, that statement was spoken by the Bodhisatta while he was still unenlightened, prior to his awakening, with reference to his status as a teacher.
“Great King, there were five teachers before his full enlightenment, while he was still a Bodhisatta who had not yet awakened, instructed by whom the Bodhisatta spent his days here and there.
What are these five?
They were those eight brahmins, Great King, who, as soon as the Bodhisatta was born, examined his marks, namely:”
Rāma, Dhaja, Lakkhaṇa, Mantī, Yañña, Suyāma, Subhoja, and Sudatta—having proclaimed his safety, they performed the protective rites; they were the first teachers.
Furthermore, Great King, at that time the Bodhisatta’s father, King Suddhodana, [was] of noble birth...

Having brought a brahmin named Sabbamitta—one of noble birth from the north, a master of the *padaka* and *veyyākaraṇa*, endowed with the sixfold analytical knowledge—and having poured water from a golden pitcher, he gave him [the child], saying, “Teach this prince”; this was the second teacher.

Furthermore, Great King, there was that deity who inspired the Bodhisatta; hearing whose words the Bodhisatta was moved and agitated, and at that very moment went forth into homelessness; this was the third teacher.
Furthermore, Great King, Āḷāra Kālāma taught the preparatory exercise for the base of nothingness; he was the fourth teacher.
Furthermore, Great King, Udaka Rāmaputta taught the preparatory exercise for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he was the fifth teacher.
These, Great King, were the five teachers prior to my enlightenment, while I was still a Bodhisatta and had not yet attained full awakening.
And those teachers [taught] worldly phenomena.
But regarding this supramundane phenomenon, Great King, for the penetration of omniscient knowledge, there is no unsurpassed instructor for the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata, Great King, is self-become and has no teacher. For that reason, it was said by the Tathāgata:
“I have no teacher, and one like me is not to be found;
in this world with its devas, [I am peerless].”
“There is no one who is my equal.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
This is the eleventh dilemma, concerning teachers and non-teachers.
The fifth chapter: On Acquaintances.
Its summary verse:
In this chapter there are eleven questions.
The Questions of Meṇḍaka are finished.
